stem: What does Twain's description show about Virginia City, Nevada, in 1863?

stimulus.source_note: Mark Twain, Roughing It (1872), ch. 52. Public domain. Text verified against the Standard Ebooks edition (standardebooks.org/ebooks/mark-twain/roughing-it/text/chapter-52).
stimulus.text:
Mark Twain, Roughing It (1872), Chapter 52, on Virginia City, Nevada:

"The year 1863 was perhaps the very top blossom and culmination of the 'flush times.' Virginia swarmed with men and vehicles to that degree that the place looked like a very hive—that is when one's vision could pierce through the thick fog of alkali dust that was generally blowing in summer... Speculation ran riot, and yet there was a world of substantial business going on, too. All freights were brought over the mountains from California (150 miles) by pack-train partly, and partly in huge wagons drawn by such long mule teams that each team amounted to a procession... All the bullion was shipped in bars by stage to San Francisco... There were three stages a day, each way, and I have seen the out-going stages carry away a third of a ton of bullion each, and more than once I saw them divide a two-ton lot and take it off."

"All along under the center of Virginia and Gold Hill, for a couple of miles, ran the great Comstock silver lode — a vein of ore from fifty to eighty feet thick between its solid walls of rock — a vein as wide as some of New York's streets."

"Virginia was a busy city of streets and houses above ground. Under it was another busy city, down in the bowels of the earth, where a great population of men thronged in and out among an intricate maze of tunnels and drifts, flitting hither and thither under a winking sparkle of lights, and over their heads towered a vast web of interlocking timbers that held the walls of the gutted Comstock apart."

options.text: It was a quiet farming village with almost no trade
options.misconception: Background: Twain describes a hive of men and vehicles, freight wagons, and stages, not a quiet farming village.

options.text: It was a government fort built to protect settlers from attack
options.misconception: Background: Virginia City was a mining boomtown, not a military fort.

options.text: It was a booming mining town built over the Comstock silver lode
It was a railroad town with no mines of its own
options.misconception: Background: the town sat directly over the Comstock lode; the railroad served the mines, it did not replace them.

rationales.A: Background: Twain's Virginia swarms with men, vehicles, and freight wagons. Nothing about it is quiet or agricultural.
rationales.B: Background: the town grew from the silver strike, not from a fort. Its business was mining, freight, and speculation.
rationales.C: Twain lays it out: a hive of a town above ground, and below it a second city of tunnels in the Comstock lode, a vein fifty to eighty feet thick.
rationales.D: Background: the lode ran under the center of Virginia and Gold Hill. The mines were the town's reason for existing.
rationales.general:
A boomtown announces itself in noise and crowds, and Twain counts both.
1. Listen to the surface: men, vehicles, dust, freight wagons, stages, all moving at once.
2. Look underneath: a second city of tunnels and timbers in a silver vein as wide as a New York street.
3. Name the place. A mining town, built on silver and crowded with people chasing it.
Remember: a boomtown is a crowd standing on top of a resource.
